content: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is a condition characterized by symptoms such as irregular or absent menstrual periods (oligo-amenorrhoea), infertility, and excessive hair growth (hirsutism). Conventional treatments for PCOS include oral medications, lifestyle modifications, and surgical interventions. Beta-endorphin, a neuropeptide, is found in the follicular fluid of both normal and polycystic ovaries. Research has shown that beta-endorphin levels in the follicular fluid of women undergoing ovulation are significantly higher than those in their plasma. Since acupuncture has been shown to influence beta-endorphin production, which in turn may affect the secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), it has been hypothesized that acupuncture could play a role in inducing ovulation by increasing beta-endorphin levels and modulating GnRH secretion. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture as a treatment for women with PCOS who experience irregular or absent ovulation, focusing on both fertility outcomes and symptom management. The researchers conducted a systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from various databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CNKI, CBM, and VIP. The search was current up to May 2018 for most databases, with the CBM search extending to November 2015. Only RCTs were included, while quasior pseudo-RCTs were excluded. The review included eight RCTs involving 1,546 women. Five of these studies were part of a previous review, while three were newly added. The studies compared true acupuncture with sham acupuncture (three RCTs), relaxation (one RCT), clomiphene (one RCT), low-frequency electroacupuncture with physical exercise or no intervention (one RCT), and true acupuncture with Diane-35 (two RCTs). Notably, the studies comparing true acupuncture with Diane-35 focused on symptom control rather than fertility outcomes. Seven of the included studies were found to have a high risk of bias in at least one domain. For the comparison of true acupuncture versus sham acupuncture, the evidence did not allow for the exclusion of clinically significant differences in live birth rates (risk ratio [RR] 0.97, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.76 to 1.24; one RCT, 926 women; low-quality evidence), multiple pregnancy rates (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.33 to 2.45; one RCT, 926 women; low-quality evidence), ovulation rates (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.02, 95% CI -0.15 to 0.19; two RCTs, 1,010 women; low-quality evidence), clinical pregnancy rates (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.29; three RCTs, 1,117 women; low-quality evidence), or miscarriage rates (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.56; one RCT, 926 women; low-quality evidence). However, the number of intermenstrual days appeared to improve in participants receiving true acupuncture compared to sham acupuncture (mean difference [MD] -312.09 days, 95% CI -344.59 to -279.59; one RCT, 141 women; low-quality evidence). Adverse events were more likely to occur in the true acupuncture group compared to the sham acupuncture group (RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.31; three RCTs, 1,230 women; moderate-quality evidence). For other comparisons, such as physical exercise or no intervention, relaxation, and clomiphene, no data were reported on live birth rates or multiple pregnancy rates. Studies involving Diane-35 did not measure fertility outcomes, as the participants in these trials were not seeking fertility treatment. The evidence was inconclusive regarding whether acupuncture improved ovulation rates (measured by ultrasound three months post-treatment) compared to relaxation (MD 0.35, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.56; one RCT, 28 women; very low-quality evidence) or Diane-35 (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.87 to 2.42; one RCT, 58 women; very low-quality evidence). Overall, the quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate. The main limitations included the failure to report critical clinical outcomes and significant imprecision in the results. Adverse events associated with acupuncture were reported in comparisons with physical exercise or no intervention, clomiphene, and Diane-35. These adverse events included dizziness, nausea, and subcutaneous hematoma. The limited number of RCTs in this area restricts the ability to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of acupuncture for PCOS.
